claim: The disbursement problem was misattributed. Banks were declining 83 of every 100 applications, and the business treated that as an external constraint on underwriting rather than an internal routing failure it could act on.
quote: When a systemic failure is attributed to uncontrollable external factors, it stops generating problem-solving energy. The first job of analysis is often to reattribute cause.

claim: Most of the failure data was unusable. Of 14,022 rejections only 6,240 carried a structured reason; the rest were blank or generic codes with no diagnostic value.

numbers.metric: share of structured rejections from the top 4 reasons

claim: Income stability predicted approval far better than declared income. A Salary Regularity Score built from 6 months of credit consistency separated the top and bottom bands by more than 66 percentage points of approval rate — and it was absent from the routing logic entirely.

numbers.metric: approval-rate gap, top vs bottom Salary Regularity band

quote: A person who earns ₹60,000 a month consistently for 24 months is completely different from a person who earned ₹60,000 last month after 18 months of ₹35,000. Declared income looks the same in both cases.

claim: Applicants underreported obligations by an average of 8.4 percentage points of FOIR. Bank-statement analysis was consistently more predictive than anything declared.
quote: When you have access to behavioural data, always prefer it to self-reported data.

claim: Asking for a bank statement upfront got 35% compliance. Showing a preliminary eligibility range first, then asking to unlock the exact offer, took it to 71% — the same ask, reframed from a compliance step into an unlock.

Turning a rejection into a pathway recovered borrowers nobody was counting. Rejected applicants given a specific reason and a re-apply timeline came back at 28%, and 67% of those cleared the eligibility filter on the second attempt.
Routing to fewer banks beat routing to many. The industry practice of firing one application at eight lenders inflated enquiry counts, which itself flagged the borrower as risky.
quote: Routing to one bank with 75% confidence is better than routing to eight banks with 20% confidence each. The math is similar but the quality signal is completely different.

claim: One bank partner rejected the enriched application packet outright and stayed resistant for eight months. More data did not change their mind; comparative outcomes from other partners did.
quote: When a stakeholder doesn't trust your methodology, more data usually isn't the answer. What changes minds is time, comparative evidence, and a relationship where they don't feel threatened.

claim: Two weeks went into assembling a clean dataset of roughly 22,000 prior applications before proposing anything. The target set afterwards — 70% disbursement against an industry range of 20-35% — was chosen to force a different operating model rather than to be achievable.
The insurance conversion rate was 0.007% and had seven separate causes, not one. Each leak cut conversion by 60-80% on its own; compounded, they produced seven purchases per hundred thousand users.
quote: When you see a deeply poor outcome, your instinct is to look for the single cause. Usually there isn't one. There are seven moderate failures compounding.

claim: The renewal form was 23 fields across 6 steps and took 11 minutes on a mid-range Android handset, timed. It went to 4 fields and one step for most renewals, using registration data the insurer already held.

Not supporting UPI was the single most expensive omission in the funnel. Card and net banking were the only options in a market where the buying demographic pays by UPI. Integration took six weeks, and 73% of purchases came through UPI in the first month after launch.

Trust was a conversion lever, not a brand exercise. Showing insurer brand names lifted quote acceptance 34%, and surfacing the IRDAI-mandated claim settlement ratio next to the price broke the market's habit of treating insurance as a pure price comparison.

numbers.metric: quote acceptance from insurer brand visibility
claim settlement ratio range across major insurers

claim: Timing beat messaging. A user whose insurance expired three days ago converted at 4.8 times the rate of one with 60 days remaining, on identical copy. The same notification also lifted 30-day retention 2.4 times against users who checked renewal unprompted.
quote: Meeting a user at the exact moment they have a need — not before, not after — is the highest-leverage intervention in conversion optimisation.

claim: Facebook interest targeting looked fine on cost per install and was catastrophic on cost per purchase — 5 times Google Search intent and 12 times organic. Cutting it from 40% of paid budget to 12% took blended cost per purchase from about ₹1,100 to about ₹590 in three months, with no drop in conversion volume.
quote: A channel that looks cheap on the metric you measure and expensive on the metric you care about is the most common way acquisition budgets get wasted.

claim: The site had 340 indexed pages against a keyword universe of tens of thousands of queries. Building a page for each of India's Regional Transport Offices produced 1,400 pages and took monthly organic installs past 200,000 for the first time.

Cutting editorial review to hit page-count targets cost more than doing it properly. A Google update three months later stripped rankings from several page classes, and recovery meant rewriting roughly 400 pages — more total effort than building them right the first time.

numbers.metric: pages rewritten after the ranking loss

quote: Programmatic SEO is only sustainable when the content is genuinely useful. Volume without quality is a short-term gain and a long-term liability.

context: CarInfo vehicle service history feature, month 11
claim: A feature I championed reached 2.8% adoption and was killed. Maintenance logging needed repeated deliberate effort and returned nothing until enough history accumulated, so the value arrived long after the user had given up.

Letting users share a vehicle report turned a utility check into an acquisition channel. Shared reports carried 12.3% of new installs within four months, and the share grew as the behaviour became habitual.
Scaling from 3.8M to 45M+ monthly actives came from three sources in roughly equal thirds: organic search, referral and sharing, and paid acquisition buying higher-intent users than before.

The headline growth figure needs decomposing to be honest. The 1200% insurance revenue growth is the compound of a larger user base, a 457-times conversion improvement, and two new product categories. On a like-for-like passenger-vehicle basis it was closer to 2,400%, and the 680-times figure refers to one specific revenue line rather than the blended total.
quote: On a like-for-like basis the improvement was approximately 2,400% from baseline — the 680x figure that appears in summary decks refers to a specific insurance revenue line, not the blended total.

claim: The opportunity was sized before the work started. Of 3.8M monthly actives, 68% were returning users and 74% of those had insurance expired or within 90 days — about 1.9M addressable users a month. At a 2% conversion, industry-normal for mobile insurance, that was 38,000 policies monthly.

context: KNIPEX India market development, product marketing
claim: A 6-month supply chain from Germany changed how every decision got made. With that feedback loop, a wrong inventory call costs six months of recovery, so the discipline becomes investing in analysis before committing rather than iterating after.
quote: The longer the feedback loop, the more important it is to get the analysis right before acting. Any system with long feedback loops rewards upfront analysis and punishes impulsive action.

claim: Carrying the full catalogue was never viable, so the first real work was choosing what not to stock. Of roughly 1,200 SKUs we prioritised 85 — under 8% — against the highest-probability commercial opportunities for the market's development stage.

Launching a cheaper line to chase a distributor's forecast damaged the premium position and the forecast never materialised. We sold 23% of the order in twelve months and discontinued the line within nine.
quote: Price positioning is not just a commercial decision. It is a brand decision with long-lasting consequences. Once you compete at a lower price point, re-establishing a premium position is extremely difficult.

claim: Professionals bought after using the tool, not after hearing about it. Hands-on demonstration reached over 4,000 professionals directly, converted 22% of them, and produced an 81% reorder rate among first-time purchasers.

Institutional trust in Indian B2B ran on a ladder that took 18 to 36 months to climb, with no shortcuts. Every attempt to accelerate it with discounts produced relationships that collapsed the moment the discount ended.

numbers.metric: time from first contact to specified-by-name

claim: Tracking infrastructure project announcements rather than waiting for sales data surfaced the data-centre construction boom as a tool-demand opportunity eight months before it appeared in our own numbers.

numbers.metric: lead time on the demand signal

context: UpGrowth, Product Head across four product lines
claim: Three teams shipped in the same week without knowing it, and the collision was organisational rather than technical. A critical bug hit about 8,000 daily actives, a CRM change invalidated an enterprise workflow, and five urgent escalations landed before lunch.

numbers.metric: daily active users affected by the bug

claim: Sixty days went into understanding the organisation before changing anything. Misdiagnosing an organisational problem costs at least as much as misdiagnosing a product one, and the symptoms point in the wrong direction more often.

About 40% of engineering time across the organisation was going to client-specific requests that sales had committed to and nobody had tested against product strategy. The problem was not that clients asked; it was that there was no mechanism for deciding.

numbers.metric: engineering time on unevaluated client requests

claim: Aggregating independently-set team OKRs produced 11 objectives and 34 key results, which is a project tracker with aspirational language rather than OKRs. Replacing it with three annual company objectives and quarterly goals linked to them restored the connection between daily work and direction.
quote: Genuine OKRs require ruthless constraint: three to five objectives maximum, each with two to three key results.

claim: Three artefacts fixed decision coherence: a 3-page quarterly Strategic Brief shared with the whole organisation, a 60-minute bi-weekly cross-team roadmap sync with a fixed agenda, and a Decision Log recording what was decided, why, and what was rejected.

Two small teams solved problems no product-line team would own. A platform team of three engineers and a PM held API contracts and technical coherence without shipping user-facing features, and a four-person enterprise team owned the cross-product experience enterprise clients actually used.

Quarterly OKRs were the wrong instrument for capabilities that took six to nine months to build and validate. They created artificial checkpoints that rewarded short-term measurable wins over strategically important progress.

context: UpGrowth, the metric I did not have
claim: The measurement I most regret not taking rigorously was client perception of product coherence. Clients used several products, and the quality of the seams between them was the thing the whole reorganisation was meant to improve.

context: Appy Pie Connect, integrations platform, Noida
claim: Pricing an integrations platform on execution volume and connector usage rather than seats took it to roughly $60K MRR. Usage pricing suited it because the value a customer got scaled with runs, not with headcount.

Most of the workflow failures were in three places nobody owned: auth handling, webhook retries and dependency validation. Fixing them lifted workflow success 15-20% without touching the product surface.
Making failures debuggable by the customer cut sales and support effort about 25%. Idempotency, surfaced errors and retry mechanics did more for support load than any documentation would have.

Routing applicants only to lenders with high disbursement probability got bank and NBFC approval rates past 90%. The model combined CIBIL scores, 6-12 months of bank statement analysis and behavioural signals.
quote: The lender pain point was never lead volume. It was trust in lead quality.

claim: A CRM built around document verification rather than pipeline tracking raised successfully processed loan applications 45% inside three months. The bottleneck was verification communication, not lead flow.

Offline loan sourcing through 1.5M+ CSC and kiosk shops, backed by Haryana and Karnataka government programmes, reached borrowers no digital funnel was going to find — without loosening lender-grade credit quality.

context: CarInfo motor insurance, both vehicle classes
claim: Both insurance lines moved by orders of magnitude once the quote-to-redirect-to-purchase drop-offs were diagnosed: bike from about 10 a day to 6,800+, car from about 5 a day to 2,300+. The fix was CTA placement, partner sequencing and context-led nudges rather than more traffic.

Moving monetisation from paid acquisition into embedded intent-led in-app journeys cut effective CAC 25-30% and raised LTV without hurting engagement. Ten-plus insurance partners had to be sequenced for it to work.

Orchestrating triggers around policy expiry, compliance deadlines and observed intent improved monetisation readiness 60-70%, measured as quote and purchase re-entry rather than first-touch conversion.

Setting portfolio-level direction on high-intent entry points, trust signals and core journeys lifted activation depth 18-25% across four consumer and B2B platforms. The leverage was in what the four had in common, not in any one roadmap.

Moving four pods off feature output and onto outcome-driven planning raised roadmap delivery predictability about 30%. Fifty-plus engineers, designers and PMs, and the change was in what got counted as done.

One measurement framework spanning 20+ growth, retention and monetisation metrics made executive decisions roughly twice as fast. Before it, every decision started with an argument about which number was right.

Real-time data reliability improved about 80%, which is what made accurate pricing, attribution and repeat monetisation possible across three to four revenue surfaces. Unreliable data does not produce cautious pricing; it produces confident wrong pricing.
Platform-level automation carried two to three times the daily transaction volume while improving SLA adherence 25-30%. Operational leverage, not more people.

A hub-and-spoke launch with three to four anchor distributors per city, aggregating downstream vendor demand into one consolidation point, was what made direct-to-vendor fulfilment from a single Bangalore warehouse work at all.

Order intake arrived by email, phone and trade expo and was systemised into one processing workflow. Nothing about it was sophisticated; it simply made order visibility and fulfilment predictable for the first time.

Validating demand on Medium before building anything, then scaling a content platform to 10,000+ published blogs. It was also where I learned SEO and content operations by running them rather than reading about them.

A hyperlocal D2C food business at 300+ daily tiffins that unit economics told me to pivot out of. Customer feedback pointed at fresh grocery retail, and the pivot was the right call rather than a retreat.
